[Śaṅkara's commentary on 6.1.4:] 'How such an instruction is — listen, dear boy. Just as in the world, by knowing one lump of clay — which is the cause of pots, dishes, and the like — everything else, the entire class of modifications made of clay, becomes known.' How can knowledge of the cause lead to knowledge of other things [the effects]? There is no fault here — because the effect is non-different from the cause. You might think: 'When one thing is known, another is not known.' True, that would be the case if the effect were different from the cause — but the effect is not different from the cause. 'Then how does this [perception] arise in the world — that this is a modification of this cause?'

children.text: START ChUp 6,1.5
children.translated_text: [Beginning of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.5]

children.text:
yathā somyaikena lohamaṇinā sarvaṃ lohamayaṃ vijñātaṃ syāt |
vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ loham ity eva satyam || ChUp_6,1.5 ||
children.translated_text: 'Just as, dear boy, by knowing one gold nugget, everything made of gold becomes known — a modification is merely a name, a verbal handle — gold alone is the reality.' (ChUp 6.1.5)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,1.5 yathā saumyaikena lohamaṇinā suvarṇapiṇḍena sarvamanyadvikārajātaṃ kaṭakamukuṭakeyūrādi vijñātaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: [Śaṅkara's commentary on 6.1.5:] 'Just as, dear boy, by knowing one gold nugget — a lump of gold — everything else, the entire class of modifications such as bracelets, crowns, armlets, and the like, becomes known.'

children.text: vācā'rambhaṇamityādi samānam //5 //
children.translated_text: '<s>Vācārambhaṇa</s>' and so forth — the same [as before]. (5)

children.text: START ChUp 6,1.6-7
children.translated_text: [Beginning of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.6-7]

children.text:
yathā somyaikena nakhanikṛntanena sarvaṃ kārṣṇāyasaṃ vijñātaṃ syāt |
vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ kṛṣṇāyasam ity eva satyam |
evaṃ somya sa ādeśo bhavatīti || ChUp_6,1.6 ||
children.translated_text: 'Just as, dear boy, by knowing one nail-cutter, everything made of iron becomes known — a modification is merely a name, a verbal handle — iron alone is the reality. Thus, dear boy, is that instruction.' (ChUp 6.1.6)

children.text:
na vai nūnaṃ bhagavantas ta etad avediṣuḥ |
yad dhy etad avediṣyan kathaṃ me nāvakṣyan |
iti bhagavāṃs tv eva me bravītv iti |
tathā somyeti hovāca || ChUp_6,1.7 ||
children.translated_text: '"Surely those revered [teachers] did not know this. For if they had known it, how would they not have told me?" So let the Blessed One himself tell me.' 'So be it, dear boy,' he said. (ChUp 6.1.7)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,1.6,7 yathā saumyaikena nakhanikṛntanenopalakṣitena kṛṣṇāyasapiṇḍenetyarthaḥ /
sarvaṃ kārṣṇāyasaṃ kṛṣṇāyasavikārajātaṃ vijñātaṃ syāt /
samānamanyat /
anekadṛṣṭāntopādānaṃ dārṣṭāntikārekabhedānugamārthaṃ dṛḍhapratītyarthaṃ ca /
evaṃ somya sa ādeśo yo mayokto bhavatītyuktavati pitaryāhetaro na vai nūnaṃ bhagavantaḥ pūjāvanto guravo mama ye ta etadyadbhavaduktaṃ vastu nāvediṣurna vijñātavanto nūnam /
children.translated_text: 'Thus, dear boy, is that instruction which I have described' — when the father had said this, [Śvetaketu] said: 'Surely those revered — honored — teachers of mine did not know this thing that you have described.'

children.text: yadyadi hyavediṣyan viditavanta etadvastu kathaṃ me guṇavate bhaktāyānugatāya nāvakṣyannoktavantastenāhaṃ manye na viditavanta iti /
children.translated_text: 'For if they had known — been aware of — this thing, how would they not have told me — one who is virtuous, devoted, and faithful?' Therefore, 'I conclude that they did not know it.'

children.text: avācyamapi gurornyagbhāvamavādītpunargurukulaṃ prati preṣaṇabhayāt /
children.translated_text: He spoke disparagingly of his teachers — which is itself improper — out of fear of being sent back to the teacher's household.

children.text: ato bhagavāṃstveva me mahyaṃ tadvastu yena sarvajñatvaṃ jñātena me syāttadbravītu kathayatvityuktaḥ pitovāca tathāstu saumyeti //6-7 //
children.translated_text: 'Therefore, let the Blessed One himself tell me — to me — that thing by knowing which I would become omniscient; let him explain it' — thus requested, the father said: 'So be it, dear boy.' (6-7)

[Śaṅkara's commentary on 6.1.6-7:] 'Just as, dear boy, by knowing one nail-cutter' — indicated [here is] a lump of iron (kṛṣṇāyasa), this is the meaning. 'Everything made of iron — the entire class of modifications of iron — becomes known.' The rest is the same. The use of multiple illustrations is for the purpose of showing that [just as] the examples have no [real] diversity, so too the illustrated [principle applies uniformly] — and for the purpose of firm conviction.

children.text: iti cchāndogyopaniṣadi ṣaṣṭhādhyāyasya prathamaḥ khaṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first section of the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

children.text: START ChUp 6,2.1
children.translated_text: [Beginning of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1]

children.text:
sad eva somyedam agra āsīd ekam evādvitīyam |
tad dhaika āhur asad evedam agra āsīd ekam evādvitīyam |
tasmād asataḥ saj jāyata || ChUp_6,2.1 ||
children.translated_text: 'In the beginning, dear boy, this [universe] was Being (<s>Sat</s>) alone, one only, without a second. Some say: "In the beginning, this was Non-being (<s>Asat</s>) alone, one only, without a second. From that Non-being, Being was born."' (ChUp 6.2.1)

children.translated_text: Therefore, this sentence 'it was merely <s>asat</s>' and the like is employed for the purpose of removing the erroneous apprehension of the person.

children.text: darśayitvā hi viparītagrahaṇaṃ tato nivartayituṃ śakyata ityarthavattvādasadādivākyasya śrautatvaṃ prāmāṇyaṃ ca siddhamityadoṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: For having shown the erroneous apprehension, it is possible to remove it from that — thus, because the sentence about <s>asat</s> and the like is meaningful, its being <s>śruti</s> (scriptural) and its authoritativeness are established — hence there is no defect.

children.text: tasmādasataḥ sarvābhāvarūpātsadvidyamānamajāyata samutpannam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, from <s>asat</s> — which is of the nature of complete non-existence — <s>Sat</s>, the existent, was born, was produced.

children.text: aḍabhāvaśchāndasaḥ //1 //
children.translated_text: The dropping of the augment (<s>aḍ</s>) is a Vedic irregularity. (1)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.2.1:] '<s>Sat</s> (Being) alone' — <s>sat</s> means a thing that is merely existent, subtle, without distinctions, all-pervading, one, untainted, without parts — it is pure consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>) that is understood from all the <s>Vedānta</s> texts. The word 'eva' (alone) is for the purpose of exclusion. What is being excluded? He says: this world, which is perceived as having names, forms, and actions — which is a modification — that [world] is connected with the word 'was' (<s>āsīt</s>) by [the statement] 'was <s>Sat</s> alone.' When was it that [the world] 'was <s>Sat</s> alone'? 'In the beginning' (<s>agre</s>) — before the origination of the world. Does it not [remain <s>Sat</s>] even now, that it is qualified by [the phrase] 'in the beginning it was'? No. Then what is the qualification? Even now, this [world] is indeed <s>Sat</s> alone, but being qualified by name and form, it becomes the object of the cognition and word 'this.' Before origination, however, it was apprehensible merely through the word and cognition '<s>Sat</s>' alone — thus the exclusion '<s>Sat</s> alone was this in the beginning' is made. For before origination, the thing cannot be grasped as having name and form — just as in the state of deep sleep. Just as one who has risen from deep sleep understands that in deep sleep there was merely pure being (<s>sattva-mātra</s>) alone — similarly, before origination — this is the purport. Just as it is said in the world: a person seeing a potter's lump of clay spread out in the morning by a potter who desires to create pots and the like, goes to another village and returns in the afternoon, and seeing the product differentiated into many forms such as pots and dishes, says 'This pot and dish and the like was merely clay alone in the morning' — similarly here too it is said 'In the beginning, this was <s>Sat</s> alone.' 'One only' — meaning there was nothing else falling within the scope of its own effect, hence 'one only' is said. 'Without a second' — just as, apart from clay, a second thing in the form of an efficient cause such as a potter who transforms [clay] into pot-forms and the like is seen [to exist] apart from clay, similarly a second thing — another entity serving as a cooperative cause — apart from <s>Sat</s>, is precluded by 'without a second.' It has no second entity — hence 'without a second.' Now, even in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system, co-referentiality with <s>sat</s> can be established for everything, since the word and cognition '<s>sat</s>' persists across substance, quality, and the rest — as seen in expressions like '<s>sat</s>-substance,' '<s>sat</s>-quality,' '<s>sat</s>-action,' and so on. True, it would be so now; but before origination, the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> do not accept that 'this effect was <s>Sat</s> alone,' because they accept the non-existence of the effect before origination. Nor do they accept that before origination [there was] one only <s>Sat</s> without a second. Therefore, the <s>Sat</s> spoken of here as the cause is different from the <s>Sat</s> conceived by the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s>, as [shown] from the examples of clay and the like. Now, regarding the determination of the nature of the thing before origination — certain <s>Vaināśikas</s> (Buddhists) say, while determining the nature [of things]: 'Before origination, this world was merely the absence of <s>Sat</s> — non-being (<s>asat</s>) — one only and without a second.' For the Buddhists conceive that the reality before origination is merely the absence of being. However, they do not accept another entity opposed to <s>Sat</s>. Just as that which is apprehended as both '<s>sat</s>' and '<s>asat</s>' — the <s>Naiyāyikas</s> [hold that] the reality is the opposite of that which is as it is. Now, if the <s>Vaināśikas</s> intend that before origination there was merely the absence of <s>Sat</s>, how can they speak of temporal relation ('before origination this was'), numerical relation ('one only'), and the quality of being 'without a second'? Indeed, this is not proper for those who accept merely being and non-being. Even the acceptance of mere non-being is improper, since without an acceptor there can be no acceptance. If [one says] the acceptor exists now but is not accepted as existing before origination — no, because there is no evidence for the absence of <s>Sat</s> before origination; the supposition that 'before origination it was merely <s>asat</s>' is untenable. Now, how can word-meaning and sentence-meaning be established for '<s>asat</s>, one only, without a second' if [the word <s>asat</s>] refers to the form of a real entity? If this cannot be established, then this sentence would become non-authoritative — [this objection is raised]. This is no defect. Because the sentence is aimed at removing the apprehension of <s>Sat</s>. The word '<s>sat</s>' denotes the form of being. 'One only, without a second' — these are co-referential with the word '<s>sat</s>.' And likewise 'this was.' Therein, the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>), employed in the sentence about <s>Sat</s>, relying on the very sentence about <s>Sat</s>, removes from the object of the cognition of the sentence about <s>Sat</s> — a cognition characterized as 'this was <s>Sat</s>, one only, without a second' — just as a person mounted on a horse, holding onto the horse, turns the horse away from objects toward which [the horse is heading] — similarly. But it does not denote the mere absence of <s>Sat</s>.

children.translated_text: Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.2.2

children.text:
kutas tu khalu somyaivaṃ syād iti hovāca |
katham asataḥ saj jāyeta |
sat tv eva somyedam agra āsīd ekam evādvitīyam || ChUp_6,2.2 ||
children.translated_text: '"But how indeed, dear boy, could it be thus?" he said. "How could being (<s>sat</s>) be born from non-being (<s>asat</s>)? No, dear boy, in the beginning this was Being (<s>Sat</s>) alone, one only, without a second."' (<s>ChUp</s> 6.2.2)

children.translated_text: This is no defect.

children.text: rajjvādyavayavebhyaḥ sarpādisaṃsthānavadbuddhipārikalpitebhyaḥ sadavayavebyo vikārasaṃsthānopapatteḥ /
children.translated_text: Because the modification-configuration is possible from the parts of <s>Sat</s> that are conceptually constructed by the intellect — just as the configuration of a snake and the like [is possible] from the parts of a rope and the like.

children.text: vācā'rambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ mṛttiketyeva satyamevaṃ sadeva satyamiti śruteḥ /
children.translated_text: 'A modification is a mere verbal designation; only clay is the reality' — since the <s>śruti</s> states that '<s>Sat</s> alone is the reality,' [this is established] thus.

children.text: ekamevādvitīyaṃ paramārthata idaṃbuddhikāle 'pi //2 //
children.translated_text: 'One only, without a second' — in ultimate reality, even at the time of the cognition 'this.' (2)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.2.2:] Having thus shown the great <s>Vaināśika</s> (Buddhist) position — the erroneous apprehension — he refutes it: 'But from what evidence (<s>pramāṇa</s>), dear boy, could it be thus — that from <s>asat</s>, <s>sat</s> is born?' — how could this be? From no evidence whatsoever could it be thus — this is the meaning. Even the observation that a sprout is seen to arise from the destruction of a seed, [and so] from non-existence — this too contradicts their own position. How? Those very parts of the seed that are characterized by the particular configuration of the seed — they continue to persist in the sprout as well; it is not the case that the sprout is born from their destruction. And the particular shape-configuration of the seed — apart from the parts of the seed — is not accepted by the <s>Vaināśikas</s> as being a real entity that would be destroyed at the birth of the sprout. If it does exist as a real entity apart from the parts, then there would be a contradiction with their own position. If [they say] that the seed-configuration is accepted conventionally (<s>saṃvṛti</s>) and is destroyed — what is this 'convention' (<s>saṃvṛti</s>)? Is it non-being or being? If non-being, then there is no example. If being, then even so, the sprout does not arise from non-being — for the sprout arises from the parts of the seed. If [they say] the parts too are destroyed — no, because the same [argument] applies to the parts of those parts. Just as for the <s>Vaināśikas</s> the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) characterized by the seed-configuration does not exist, similarly the parts too [would not exist] — hence the impossibility of their destruction as well. Since the parts of the seed also have subtle parts, and those parts have even subtler parts — and since this regress never terminates — the impossibility of destruction applies everywhere. Since the cognition of '<s>sat</s>' (being) persists [throughout], the being-ness never ceases — thus for the proponents of <s>sat</s> (<s>sadvāda</s>), the origination of <s>sat</s> from <s>sat</s> alone will be established. But for the proponents of <s>asat</s> (<s>asadvāda</s>), there is no example of <s>sat</s> arising from <s>asat</s>. For the <s>sadvādins</s>, the origination of a pot from a lump of clay is observed — since [the pot] exists when that [clay] exists and is absent when that [clay] is absent. If the pot were produced from mere non-existence, one desiring a pot would not take up a lump of clay. And the persistence of the word and cognition of non-existence would apply to pots and the like [which is absurd]. But this is not the case — therefore there is no origination of <s>sat</s> from <s>asat</s>. As for their statement that 'the cognition of clay is the cause of the cognition of pot' — meaning the cognition of clay is said to be the cause of the cognition of pot, but neither clay nor pot truly exists in the ultimate sense — even so, the cognition of clay, being existent, is the cause of the cognition of pot which is also existent — hence there is no origination of <s>sat</s> from <s>asat</s>. If [they say] there is merely temporal sequence between the cognitions of clay and pot as cause-occasion and occasioned, but not a cause-effect relation — no, because the <s>Vaināśikas</s> have no external example for the mere succession of cognitions. Therefore, 'But how indeed, dear boy, could it be thus?' he said — 'How, by what means, could <s>sat</s> be born from <s>asat</s>?' The purport is that there is no example whatsoever for the origination of <s>sat</s> from <s>asat</s>. Having thus refuted the <s>asadvāda</s> position, he concludes with the establishment of his own position: 'In the beginning, this was Being (<s>Sat</s>) alone, dear boy.' Now, even for the <s>sadvādin</s>, there is no example of <s>sat</s> originating from <s>sat</s> — since the origination of another pot from a pot is not observed. True, it is so — <s>sat</s> does not produce another <s>sat</s>; rather, <s>sat</s> itself persists in another configuration — just as a snake coils itself up, and just as clay [manifests] through the different forms of lump, pot, potsherd, and so on. If so — if <s>Sat</s> persists through all configurations — how [can it be said] 'In the beginning, this was'? It is answered: Have you not heard that this is the exclusion of the effect denoted by the word 'this' [from the word] '<s>Sat</s> alone'? Then it would follow that before origination, it was <s>asat</s> alone — [meaning] that which is now denoted by 'this' did not exist, and now 'this' has come into being. No — because <s>Sat</s> itself persists as the object of the word and cognition 'this' — just as clay itself persists as the object of the words and cognitions 'lump,' 'pot,' and so on. Now, just as clay is an entity, so too lump, pot, and the like [are entities]; similarly, since the cognition of the effect is the object of a cognition other than the cognition of <s>Sat</s>, the effect that has arisen would be another, different entity from <s>Sat</s> — like a cow is different from a horse. No — because although lump, pot, and the like deviate from each other, they do not deviate from clay-ness. Even though a pot deviates from a lump and a lump from a pot, they do not deviate from clay-ness — therefore lump and pot are merely clay. (But a cow deviates from a horse and a horse from a cow.) Therefore, pots and the like are merely configurations of clay and the like. Similarly, all this is merely a configuration of <s>Sat</s> — thus it is proper [to say] 'Before origination, this was <s>Sat</s> alone,' since a modification that is merely a configuration is merely a verbal designation (<s>vācārambhaṇa-mātra</s>). Now, <s>Sat</s> is without parts — 'without parts, without action, peaceful, without blemish, untainted' — 'The divine <s>Puruṣa</s> is indeed formless, both external and internal, unborn' — from such <s>śruti</s> passages, how can a modification-configuration be possible for <s>Sat</s> which is without parts?

children.translated_text: 'That [Being] willed: "May I become many, may I be born forth." It created fire (<s>tejas</s>). That fire willed: "May I become many, may I be born forth." It created water (<s>āpas</s>). Therefore, wherever a person grieves or perspires, from fire alone is water born.' (<s>ChUp</s> 6.2.3)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,2.3 tatsadaikṣatekṣāṃ darśanaṃ kṛtavat /

children.translated_text: 'May I become many, may I be born' — as before.

children.text: tadapo 'sṛjata /
children.translated_text: It created water (<s>āpas</s>).

children.text: āpo dravāḥ snigdhāḥ syandinyaḥ śuklāśceti prasiddhā loke /
children.translated_text: Water is well known in the world as liquid, unctuous, flowing, and white in color.

children.text: yasmāttejasaḥ kāryabhūtā āpastasmādyatra kvaca deśe kāle vā śocati santapyate svedate prasvidyate vā puruṣastejasa eva tattadā'po 'dhijāyante //3//
children.translated_text: Because water is the effect of fire, therefore wherever and whenever a person grieves, is heated, sweats, or perspires — from fire itself, at that time water is produced. (3)

[Śaṅkara's commentary on 6.2.3:] That Sat (Being) saw (aikṣata) — it performed seeing, deliberation. And therefore, Pradhāna (primordial matter) as conceived by the Sāṃkhyas is not the cause of the world, because Pradhāna is accepted as non-conscious. But this Sat is conscious, since it is the seer (īkṣitṛ). How did it see? — 'May I become many, may I be born, may I be produced abundantly.' Just as clay takes the form of pots and such, or just as a rope appears in the form of a snake and the like, superimposed by the intellect. Is then everything that is perceived unreal, like a rope appearing in the form of a snake superimposed by the intellect? No — because Sat (Being) itself is apprehended otherwise through the appearance of duality; we say that there is no non-existence of anything anywhere. The logicians (tārkikas) postulate another substance different from Sat and then assert its non-existence before its origination and after its destruction — we do not in any way, at any time, postulate any substance of designation or designated object different from Sat. Rather, everything that is designated and spoken of through the notion of 'other' is Sat alone. Just as a rope itself, through the notion of a snake, is designated as 'snake'; or just as a lump, pot, and such, through the notion of something other than clay, are designated in the world by the words 'lump,' 'pot,' and so on. But for those who discern the distinction of the rope, the designation and cognition of 'snake' cease; and just as for those who discern the distinction of clay, the words and cognitions of 'pot' and such cease — so too for those who discern the distinction of Sat, the words and cognitions of other modifications cease. This is established from śrutis such as 'From which words turn back, not reaching it together with the mind,' and 'In the indescribable, in the unsupported,' and so on. Having thus deliberated, that Sat created tejas (fire/heat) — it created fire. But one might object: in another śruti, 'From this Ātman indeed, space came into being,' space is heard to come from Ātman, then wind from space, and fire as the third — but here, how is fire created first from that Sat, and space from that same source? This is contradictory. There is no defect — because it is possible to supply the understanding that 'that Sat created fire' occurs after the creation of space and wind. Or alternatively, the order of creation is not intended here; rather, what is intended is that all this is an effect of Sat, and therefore Sat is one alone without a second — from the analogy of clay and such. Or else, since trivṛtkaraṇa (tripartite combination) is what is intended, the text describes only the creation of fire, water, and food. Fire (tejas) is well known in the world as that which burns, cooks, illuminates, and is red in color. That Sat, having created fire, saw — meaning Sat, abiding in the form of fire, saw.

children.text: tā āpa aikṣanta bahvayaḥ syāma prajāyemahīti tā annamasṛjanta tasmādyatra
children.translated_text: 'Those waters saw: "May we become many, may we be born." They created food. Therefore, wherever it rains, there indeed food becomes most abundant. From water alone is edible food produced.' (ChUp 6.2.4)

children.text: kva ca varṣati tadeva bhūyiṣṭhamannaṃ bhavatyadbhya eva tadadhyannādyaṃ jāyate //4//
children.translated_text: [continuation of 6.2.4 root text]
[<s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.2.4]

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,2.4 tā āpa aikṣanta pūrvavadevābākārasaṃsthitaṃ sadaikṣatetyarthaḥ /
bahvayaḥ prabhūtāḥ syāma bhavema prajāyemahi utpadyemahoti /
tā annamasṛjanta pṛthivīlakṣaṇam /
pārthivaṃ hyannaṃ yasmādapkāryamannaṃ tasmādyatra kva ca varṣati deśe tattatraiva bhūyiṣṭhaṃ prabūtamannaṃ bhavati /
ato 'dbhya eva tadannādyamadhijāyate /
tā annamasṛjanteti pṛthivyuktā pūrvamiha tu dṛṣṭānte 'nnaṃ ca tadādyaṃ ceti viśeṣaṇādvrīhiyavādyā ucyante /
annaṃ ca guru sthiraṃ dhāraṇaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ ca rūpataḥ prasiddham /
nanu tejaḥ prabhṛtiṣvīkṣaṇaṃ na gamyate hiṃsādipratiṣedhābhāvāttrāsādikāryānupalambhācca tatra kathaṃ tatteja aikṣatetyādi /
neṣa doṣaḥ /
īkṣitṛkāraṇapariṇāmatvāttejaḥ prabhṛtīnāṃ sata ivekṣiturniyatakramaviśiṣṭakāryotpādakatvāt tejaḥ prabhṛtīkṣata ivekṣata ityucyate bhūtam /
nanu sato 'pyupacaritamevekṣitṛtvam /
na /
sadīkṣaṇasya kevalaśabdagamyatvānna śakyamupacaritaṃ kalpayitum /
tejaḥ prabhṛtīnāṃ tvanumīyate mukhyekṣaṇābhāva iti yuktamupacaritaṃ kalpayitum /
nanu sato 'pi mṛdvatkāraṇatvādacetanatvaṃ śakyamanumātum /
ataḥ pradhānasyaivācetanasya sataścetanārthatvānniyatakālakramaviśiṣṭakāryotpādakatvāccaikṣatevaikṣateti śakyamanumātumupacaritamevekṣaṇam /
dṛṣṭaśca loke 'cetane cetanavadupacāraḥ /
yathā kūlaṃ pipatiṣatīti tadvatsato 'pi syāt /
na /
tatsatyaṃ sa ātmeti tasminnātmopadeśāt /
ātmopadeśo 'pyupacarita iti cedyathā mamā'tmā bhadrasena iti ātmanaḥ sarvārthakāriṇyanātmanyātmopacārastadvat /
na /
sadasmīti satsatyābhisandhasya"tasya tāvadeva ciram" iti mokṣopadeśāt /
so 'pyupacāra iti cet /
pradhānātmābhisandhasya mokṣasāmīpyaṃ vartata iti mokṣopadeśo 'pyupacarita eva /
yathā loke grāmaṃ gantuṃ prasthitaḥ prāptavānahaṃ grāmamiti brūyāt tvarāpekṣayā tadvat /
na /
yena vijñātenāvijñātaṃ vijñātaṃ bhavatītyupakramāt /
satyetasminvijñāte sarvaṃ vijñātaṃ bhavati tadananyatvātsarvasyādvitīyavacanācca /
na cānyadvijñātavyamavaśiṣṭaṃ śrāvitaṃ śrutyānumeyaṃ vā liṅgato 'sti yena mokṣopadeśa upacaritaḥ syāt /
children.translated_text: Nor is there anything else remaining to be known — taught by <s>śruti</s> or inferable from evidence — by which the teaching of liberation could be figurative.

children.text: sarvasya ca prapāṭhakārthasyopacaritatvaparikalpanāyāṃ vṛthā śramaḥ parikalpayituḥ syātpuruṣārthasādhanavijñānasya tarkeṇaivādhigatatvāttasya /
children.translated_text: And if the entire meaning of the chapter (<s>prapāṭhaka</s>) were construed as figurative, the effort of the construer would be futile — since the knowledge that is the means to the human goal (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) would have been attained by reasoning alone.

children.text: tasmādvedaprāmāṇyānna śrutārthaparityāgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, because of the authority of the <s>Veda</s>, the meaning taught by <s>śruti</s> should not be abandoned.

children.text: ataścetanāvatkāraṇaṃ jagata iti siddham //4//
children.translated_text: Hence it is established that the cause of the world is conscious (<s>cetana</s>). (4)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.2.4:] Those waters saw — as before, meaning <s>Sat</s>, abiding in the form of water, saw. 'May we, the abundant ones, become [many], may we be born, may we be produced.' They created food — characterized as earth. For food is earthy. Since food is the effect of water, therefore wherever it rains — in that very place, abundant food comes into being. Hence, from water alone, edible food is produced. 'They created food' — [the word 'food'] was spoken earlier as earth, but here, in the analogy, through the specification 'food and what is edible,' rice, barley, and such are meant. Food is well known as heavy, stable, supporting, and black in color. [Objection:] But in fire and the rest, seeing (<s>īkṣaṇa</s>) is not comprehended, because there is no prohibition against harm [applicable to them] and because the effects such as fear are not observed in them — so how can [the text say] 'that fire saw' and so on? There is no defect — because fire and the rest are transformations of a cause that is a seer (<s>īkṣitṛ</s>), and because, like <s>Sat</s> which is a seer, they produce effects in a fixed sequence, fire and the rest are said to see 'as if they saw.' [Objection:] But even of <s>Sat</s>, the seeing is only figurative. No — because the seeing of <s>Sat</s> is known only through scripture, it is not possible to construe it as figurative. But for fire and the rest, the absence of primary seeing is inferred — hence it is appropriate to construe it as figurative. [Objection:] But even of <s>Sat</s>, being a cause like clay, unconsciousness can be inferred. Therefore, even of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), which is unconscious, since <s>Sat</s> serves the purpose of consciousness, and since it produces effects in a fixed temporal sequence, its seeing can be inferred as figurative — 'it saw as if it saw.' And indeed, in the world, figurative attribution of consciousness to the unconscious is seen — just as [one says] 'the bank wants to fall.' So it might be with <s>Sat</s> too. No — because [the text says] 'that is the truth, that is the <s>Ātman</s>' — because of the teaching that it is the <s>Ātman</s>. [Objection:] If you say the <s>Ātman</s>-designation too is figurative — as in 'My <s>ātman</s> is <s>Bhadrasena</s>' — where the <s>ātman</s>-designation is figuratively applied to a non-self that accomplishes all purposes of the self? No — because of the teaching of liberation to one who identifies truly with <s>Sat</s>: 'I am <s>Sat</s>' — [the text says] 'for him there is only that much delay' — thus liberation is taught. [Objection:] If you say even that is figurative — that one who identifies with <s>Pradhāna</s> as self approaches liberation, and hence the teaching of liberation too is figurative — just as in the world, one who has set out for a village might say 'I have reached the village' with reference to urgency? No — because of the introductory statement: 'By knowing which the unknown becomes known' — since when this [<s>Sat</s>] is truly known, everything becomes known, because everything is non-different from it, and because of the statement that it is without a second.

children.text: iti cchāndogyopaniṣadi ṣaṣṭhādhyāyasya dvitīyaḥ khaṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second section of the sixth chapter of the <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>.

children.text: START ChUp 6,3.1
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.3.1]

children.text: teṣāṃ khalv eṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ trīṇy eva bījāni bhavanty āṇḍajaṃ jīvajam udbhijjam iti || ChUp_6,3.1 ||
children.translated_text: 'Of these beings, there are only three seeds: born from an egg (<s>āṇḍaja</s>), born from a living being (<s>jīvaja</s>), and sprouting forth (<s>udbhijja</s>).' (ChUp 6.3.1)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,3.1 teṣāṃ jīvāviṣṭānāṃ khalveṣāṃ pakṣyādīnāṃ bhūtānāmeṣāmiti pratyakṣanirdeśānna tu tejaḥprabhṛtīnāṃ teṣāṃ trivṛtkaraṇasya vakṣyamāṇatvādasati trivṛtkarame pratyakṣanirdeśānupapattiḥ /
devatāśabdaprayogācca tejaḥ prabhṛtiṣvimāstisro devatā iti /
tasmātteṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ pakṣipaśusthāvarādīnāṃ trīṇyeva nātiriktāni bījāni kāraṇāni bhavanti /
kāni tānītyucyante /
āṇḍajamaṇḍājjātamaṇḍajamaṇḍajamevā'ṇḍajaṃ pakṣyādi /
pakṣisarpādibhyo hi pakṣisarpādayo jāyamānā dṛśyante /
tena pakṣī pakṣiṇāṃ bījaṃ sarpaḥ sarpāṇāṃ tathānyadapyaṇḍājjātaṃ tajjātīyānāṃ bījamityarthaḥ /
nanvaṇḍājjātamaṇḍajamucyate 'to 'ṇḍameva bījamiti yuktaṃ kathamaṇḍajaṃ bījamucyate /
satyamevaṃ syādyadi tvadicchātantrā śrutiḥ syātstavatantrā tu śrutiryata āhā'ṇḍajādyeva bījaṃ nāṇḍādīti /
dṛśyate cāṇḍajādyabhāve tajjātīyasantatyabhāvo nāṇḍādyabhāve /
ato 'ṇḍajādīnyeva bījānyaṇḍajādīnām /
tathā jīvājjātaṃ jīvajaṃ jarāyujamityetatpuruṣapaśvādi /
children.translated_text: Likewise, <s>jīvaja</s>: born from a living being — that is, <s>jarāyuja</s> (born from a womb) — such as humans, cattle, and the like.

children.text: udbhijjamudbhinattītyudbhitsthāvaraṃ tato jātamudbhijjaṃ dhānā vodbhittato jāyata ityudbhijjaṃ sthāvarabījaṃ sthāvarāṇāṃ bījamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Udbhijja</s>: that which breaks through (<s>udbhinatti</s>), that is <s>udbhit</s> — a plant; what is born from that is <s>udbhijja</s>. Grain is <s>udbhit</s>; what is born from it is <s>udbhijja</s> — the seed of plants is the seed of plants, that is the meaning.

children.text: svedajasaṃśokajayoraṇḍajodbhijjayoreva yathāsambhavamantarbhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: The sweat-born (<s>svedaja</s>) and moisture-born (<s>saṃśokaja</s>) are included, as appropriate, within the egg-born and the sprouting-forth categories.

children.text: evaṃ hyavadhāraṇaṃ trīṇyeva bījānītyupapannaṃ bhavati //1 //
children.translated_text: Thus the definitive statement 'there are only three seeds' becomes tenable. (1)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.3.1:] 'Of these' — of these beings such as birds and others that are pervaded by the <s>jīva</s> (individual self) — [the word] 'these' (<s>eṣām</s>) indicates a proximate reference, and not to fire and the rest, because <s>trivṛtkaraṇa</s> (tripartite combination) of those is yet to be stated, and without tripartite combination, a proximate reference is untenable. And because the word 'deity' (<s>devatā</s>) is used for fire and the rest — 'these three deities.' Therefore, of these beings — birds, animals, plants, and so on — there are only three, no more, seeds, that is, causes. What are they? It is stated — <s>āṇḍaja</s>: born from an egg — <s>āṇḍaja</s> is that which is born from an egg, such as birds and the like. For birds, snakes, and such are seen to be born from birds, snakes, and such. Thus a bird is the seed of birds, a snake the seed of snakes; likewise, whatever else is born from an egg is the seed of those of the same kind — that is the meaning. [Objection:] But if what is born from an egg is called <s>āṇḍaja</s>, then it is appropriate that the egg itself is the seed — how can the egg-born [creature] be called the seed? True, it would be so if scripture were dependent on your wish; but scripture is autonomous, since it says that the egg-born and such alone are the seeds, not the egg and such. And indeed, in the absence of the egg-born and such, the continuation of that species is seen to be absent, but not in the absence of the egg and such. Therefore, the egg-born and such alone are the seeds of the egg-born and such.

children.text: START ChUp 6,3.2
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.3.2]

children.text:
seyaṃ devataikṣata |
hantāham imās tisro devatā anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇīti || ChUp_6,3.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'This deity (<s>devatā</s>) thought: "Let me enter these three deities with this living self (<s>jīva ātman</s>) and manifest name and form."' (ChUp 6.3.2)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,3.2 seyaṃ prakṛtā sadākhyā tejobannayonirdevatoktaikṣatekṣitavatī yathāpūrvaṃ bahu syāmiti /
tadeva bahubhavanaṃ prayojanaṃ nādyāpi nirvṛttamityata īkṣāṃ punaḥ kṛtavatī bahubhavanameva prayojanamurarīkṛtya /
katham /
hantedānīmahamimā yathoktāsteja ādyāstisro devatā, anena jīveneti, svabuddhisthaṃ pūrvasṛṣṭyanubhūtaprāṇadhārāṇamātmānameva smarantyāhānena jīvenā'tmaneti /
prāṇadhāraṇakartrā'tmaneti vacanātsvātmano 'vyatiriktena caitanyasvarūpatayāviśiṣṭenetyetaddarśayati /
anupraviśya, tejobannabhūtamātrāsaṃsargeṇa labdhaviśeṣavijñānā satī, nāma ca rūpaṃ ca nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi vispaṣṭamākaravā"ṇyasaunāmāyamidaṃrūpa"iti vyākuryāmityarthaḥ /
nanu na yuktamidamasaṃsāriṇyāḥ sarvajñāyā devatāyā buddhipūrvakamanekaśatasahasrānarthāśrayaṃ dehamanupraviśya duḥkhamanubhaviṣyāmīti saṅkalpanamanupraveśaśca svātantrye sati /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.3.2:] This deity under discussion, called <s>Sat</s> (Being), the source of fire, water, and food — it saw, as before, 'May I become many.' That purpose of becoming many has not yet been accomplished — therefore it deliberated again, accepting the very purpose of becoming many. How? 'Let me now enter these three deities — fire and the rest, as described — with this living self (<s>jīva ātman</s>).' Remembering its own self — the sustainer of <s>prāṇa</s> (life-force), previously experienced in prior creation as established in its own intellect — it says 'with this living self (<s>jīva ātman</s>).' By the statement 'with the self that is the agent of sustaining <s>prāṇa</s>,' it shows that [this is] through its own self, undifferentiated in its essential nature as consciousness. Having entered — having, through the combination with the elemental constituents of fire, water, and food, acquired specific cognition — 'let me manifest name and form clearly — let me distinguish "this one has this name, this one has this form"' — that is the meaning. [Objection:] But it is not proper that this deity, which is omniscient and free from <s>saṃsāra</s>, should deliberately enter a body that is the locus of hundreds of thousands of miseries and resolve 'I shall experience suffering' — if it has autonomy.

children.text:
satyamevaṃ na yuktaṃ syādyadi svenaivāvikṛtena rūpeṇānupraviśeyaṃ duḥkhamanubhaveyamiti ca saṅkalpitavatī na tvevam /
kathaṃ tarhi /
anena jīvenā'tmanānupraviśyeti vacanāt /
jīvo hi nāma devatāyā ābhāsamātram /
buddhyādibhūtamātrāsaṃsargajanita ādarśa iva praviṣṭaḥ puruṣapratibimbo jalādiṣviva ca sūryādīnām /
acintyānantaśaktimatyā devatāyā buddhyādisambandhaścaitanyābhāso devatāsvarūpavivekāgrahaṇanimittaḥ sukhī duḥkhī mūḍha ityādyanekavikalpapratyayahetuḥ /
chāyāmātreṇa jīvarūpeṇānupraviṣṭatvāddevatā na daihikaiḥ svataḥ sukha duḥkhādibhiḥ sambadhyate /
children.translated_text: Because the deity has entered only as a mere shadow in the form of the <s>jīva</s>, it is not intrinsically affected by the bodily pleasures, sufferings, and the like.

children.text: yathā puruṣādityādaya ādarśodakādiṣu cchāyāmātreṇānupraviṣṭā ādarśodakadidoṣainaṃ sambadhyante tadvaddevatāpi /
children.translated_text: Just as a person, the sun, and such, having entered mirrors, water, and the like as a mere shadow, are not affected by the defects of the mirror, water, and such — so too the deity.

children.text: sūryo yathā sarvalokasya cakṣurna lipyate cākṣuṣairbāhyadoṣaiḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Just as the sun, the eye of the entire world, is not tainted by the external defects [perceived by] the eye,

children.text: ekastathā sarvabhūtāntarātmā na lipyate lokaduḥkhena bāhyaḥ //
children.translated_text: so too the one inner <s>Ātman</s> of all beings is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external [to it].'

True, it would not be proper if it were to enter with its own unmodified form and had resolved 'I shall experience suffering.' But it is not so. How then? Because of the statement 'having entered with this living self (<s>jīva ātman</s>).' For the <s>jīva</s> is merely a reflection (<s>ābhāsa</s>) of the deity — like the reflection of a person that has entered into a mirror through the combination with the elemental constituents such as intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), or like [the reflection] of the sun and such in water and the like. The connection of the deity — which possesses inconceivable infinite power — with intellect and such [produces] a reflection of consciousness, which, due to the failure to discriminate it from the essential nature of the deity, becomes the cause of manifold conceptual cognitions such as 'happy,' 'unhappy,' 'deluded,' and so on.

children.text:
"ākāśavatsarvagataśca nityaḥ"iti ca vājasaneyake /
nanu cchāyāmātraścejjīvo mṛṣaiva prāptastayā paralokehalokādi ca tasya /
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
sadātmanā satyatvābhyupagamāt /
sarvaṃ ca nāmarūpādi sadātmanaiva satyaṃ vikārajātaṃ svastvanṛtameva /
vācā'rambhaṇa vikāro nāmadheyamityukkatvāt /
tathā jīvo 'pīti /
children.translated_text: So too the <s>jīva</s>.

children.text: yakṣānurūpo hi baliriti nyāyaprasiddhiḥ /
children.translated_text: For the maxim is well known: 'The offering corresponds to the deity (<s>yakṣa</s>).'

children.text: ataḥ sadātmanā sarvavyavahārāṇāṃ sarvavikārāmāṃ ca satyatvaṃ sato 'nyatvenānṛtatvamiti na kaściddoṣastārkikairihānuvaktuṃ śakyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, all transactions and all modifications are real by virtue of having Sat (Being) as their essence, and unreal as being other than Sat — hence no fault can be stated here by logicians.

children.text: yathetaretaraviruddhadvaitavādāḥ svabuddhivikalpamātrā atattvaniṣṭhā iti śakyaṃ vaktum //2 //
children.translated_text: Just as the mutually contradictory dualistic doctrines are mere fancies of their own intellect, not grounded in reality — so it can be stated. (2)

And in the <s>Vājasaneyi</s> [recension]: 'Like space, all-pervading and eternal.' [Objection:] But if the <s>jīva</s> is merely a shadow, then it is false — and so would be its other-world, this-world, and the like. There is no defect — because its reality is accepted through [its identity with] the <s>Sat</s>-<s>Ātman</s>. And all name and form is real only through the <s>Sat</s>-<s>Ātman</s>; the entire class of modifications is in itself unreal — because it has been said: 'A modification is a mere verbal designation, a name.'

children.text: START ChUp 6,3.3
children.translated_text: [Beginning of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.3]

children.text:
tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtam ekaikāṃ karavāṇīti |
seyaṃ devatemās tisro devatā anenaiva jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākarot || ChUp_6,3.3 ||
children.translated_text: '"Let me make each one of them tripartite" — that deity, having entered into these three deities by means of this very <s>jīva</s> (individual self), differentiated name and form.' (ChUp 6.3.3)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,3.3 saivaṃ tisro devatā anupraviśya svātmāvasthe bījabhūte avyākṛte nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇītīkṣitvā tāsāṃ ca tisṛṇāṃ devatānāmekaikāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtaṃ karavāṇi /
ekaikasyāsrivṛtkaraṇa ekaikasyāḥ prādhānyaṃ dvayordvayorguṇabhāvo 'nthathā hi rajjavā ivaikameva trivṛtkaraṇaṃ syāt na tu tisṛṇāṃ pṛthakpṛthaktrivṛtkaraṇamiti /
children.translated_text: In the tripartite making of each one, each one has predominance while the other two have a subordinate status; otherwise, as with a single rope, there would be just one tripartite making, not a separate tripartite making of each of the three.

children.text: evaṃ hi tejobannānāṃ pṛthaṅnāmapratyayalābhaḥ syātteja idamimā āpo 'nnamidamiti ca /
children.translated_text: For thus the separate apprehension of names for fire, water, and food would be possible — 'this is fire,' 'these are waters,' 'this is food.'

children.text: sati ca pṛthaṅnāmapratyayalābhe devatānāṃ samyagvyavahārasya prasiddhiḥ prayojanaṃ syāt /
children.translated_text: And when there is such separate apprehension of names, the proper conventional usage of the deities would be established — that would be the purpose.

children.text: evamīkṣitvā seyaṃ devatemāstisro devatā anenaiva yathoktenaiva jīvena sūryabimbavadantaḥ praviśya vairājaṃ piṇḍaṃ prathamaṃ devādīnāṃ ca piṇḍānanupraviśya yathāsaṅkalpameva nāmarūpe vyākarodasaunāmāyamidaṃrūpa iti //3 //
children.translated_text: Having thus reflected, that deity, having entered these three deities by means of this very <s>jīva</s> as described — having entered the body of <s>Virāj</s> first, like [entering] the orb of the sun from within, and having entered the bodies of gods and others — differentiated name and form according to its resolve: 'This one has this name, this one has this form.' (3)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.3.3:] That very [deity], having entered [these three deities], reflecting 'Let me differentiate name and form, which exist in their own essential state as seeds, in an undifferentiated condition,' and having resolved 'Let me make each one of these three deities tripartite, tripartite.'

children.text: START ChUp 6,3.4
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.3.4]

children.text:
tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtam ekaikām akarot |
yathā tu khalu somyemās tisro devatās trivṛt trivṛd ekaikā bhavati tan me vijānīhīti || ChUp_6,3.4 ||
children.translated_text: 'It made each one of them tripartite. Now learn from me, dear one, how each of these three deities becomes tripartite.' (ChUp 6.3.4)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,3.4 tāsāṃ ca devatānāṃ guṇapradhānabhāvena trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāmakarotkṛtavatī devatā /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.3.4:] Of those deities, it made each one tripartite through the relation of predominance and subordination — the deity has done so.

children.text: tiṣṭhatu tāvaddevatādipiṇḍānāṃ nāmarūpābhyāṃ vyākṛtānāṃ tejobannamayatvena tridhātvaṃ, yathā tu khalu bahurimāḥ piṇḍebhyastisro devatāsrivṛttrivṛdekaikā bhavati tanme mama nigadato vijānīhi viṣṭaspamavadhārayodāharaṇataḥ //4//
children.translated_text: Setting aside for now the tripartite nature of the bodies of deities and others — which have been differentiated by name and form — as consisting of fire, water, and food: 'Now, dear one, learn from me — from my exposition — understand distinctly through illustrations, how indeed each of these three deities in their many bodily forms becomes tripartite.' (4)

children.text: iti cchāndogyopaniṣadi ṣaṣṭhādhyāyasya tṛtīyaḥ khaṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the third section of the sixth chapter of the <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>.

children.text: START ChUp 6,4.1
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.4.1]

children.text:
yad agne rohitaṃ rūpaṃ tejasas tad rūpam |
yac chuklaṃ tad apām |
yat kṛṣṇaṃ tad annasya |
apāgād agner agnitvam |
vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇīty eva satyam || ChUp_6,4.1 ||
children.translated_text: 'The red colour of fire is the form of <s>tejas</s> (heat/light). Its white colour is that of water. Its dark colour is that of food. Thus has fire-ness departed from fire. The modification is merely a verbal designation, a name — only the three colours are real.' (ChUp 6.4.1)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,4.1 yattaddevatānāṃ trivṛtkaraṇamuktaṃ tasyaivodāharaṇamucyate /
udāharaṇaṃ nāmaikadeśaprasiddhyarthamudāhriyata iti /
tadetadāha - yadagnesrivṛtkṛtānāṃ, yatkṛṣṇaṃ tasyaivāgne rūpaṃ tadannasya pṛthivyā atrivṛtkṛtāyā iti viddhi /
tatraivaṃ sata rūpatrayavyatirekeṇāgniriti yanmanyase tvaṃ tasyāgneragnitvamidānīmapāgādapagatam /
prāgrūpatrayavivekavijñānādyāgnibuddhirāsītte sāgnibuddhirapagatāgniśabdaścetyarthaḥ /
yathādṛṣyamānaraktopadhānasaṃyuktaḥ sphaṭiko gṛhyamāṇaḥ padmarāgo 'yamitiśabdabuddhyoḥ prayojako bhavati prāgupadhānasphaṭikayorvivekavijñāne tu padmarāgaśabdabuddhī nivartete tadvivekavijñātustadvat /
nanu kimatra buddhiśabdakalpanayā kriyate prāgrūpatrayavivekakaraṇādagnirevā'sīttadagneragnitvaṃ rohitādirūpavivekakaraṇādapāgāditi yuktaṃ yathā tantvapakarṣaṇe paṭābhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Objection: What is the point of this contrivance about cognition and word? Before the separation of the three colours, it was indeed fire; the fire-ness of that fire departed through the separation of the red and other colours — just as a cloth ceases to exist when the threads are removed.

children.text: naivaṃ, buddhiśabdamātrameva hyagniryata āha vācā'rambhaṇamagnirnāma vikāro nāmadheya nāmamātramityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: Not so — for fire is merely a word and cognition, since the text says: 'The modification is merely a verbal designation (<s>vācārambhaṇa</s>), a name' — meaning it is merely a name.

children.text: ato 'gnibuddharapi mṛṣaiva /
children.translated_text: Therefore the cognition of fire too is false.

children.text: kiṃ tarhi tatra satyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇītyeva satyaṃ nāṇumātramapi rūpatrayavyatirekeṇa satyamastītyavadhāraṇārthaḥ //1 //
children.translated_text: What then is real there? 'Only the three colours are real' — [the word] 'eva' (only) is for emphatic restriction, meaning not even an atom of reality exists apart from the three colours. (1)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.4.1:] What was stated as the tripartite making of the deities — an illustration of that very thing is now given. An illustration is cited for the purpose of making a part [of the teaching] well understood. The text states: 'The red [colour] of fire' — of fire that has been made tripartite — 'the dark colour of that very fire is the form of food, of earth that has not been made tripartite' — understand it thus. This being the case, what you think of as 'fire' apart from the three colours — the fire-ness of that fire has now departed, has gone away. Before the discriminative knowledge separating the three colours, there was a cognition 'fire' — that cognition of fire and the word 'fire' have departed — this is the meaning. Just as a crystal placed upon a visible red cloth, when perceived, causes the word and cognition 'this is a ruby,' but when the distinction between the cloth and crystal is known, the word and cognition 'ruby' cease — similarly for the one who has discriminated [the three colours].

children.text: START ChUp 6,4.2
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.4.2]

children.text:
yad ādityasya rohitaṃ rūpaṃ tejasas tad rūpam |
yac chuklaṃ tad apām |
yat kṛṣṇaṃ tad annasya |
apāgād ādityād ādityatvam |
vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇīty eva satyam || ChUp_6,4.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'The red colour of the sun is the form of <s>tejas</s>. Its white colour is that of water. Its dark colour is that of food. Thus has the sun-ness departed from the sun. The modification is merely a verbal designation, a name — only the three colours are real.' (ChUp 6.4.2)

children.text:
yac candramaso rohitaṃ rūpaṃ tejasas tad rūpam |
yac chuklaṃ tad apām |
yat kṛṣṇaṃ tad annasya |
apāgāc candrāc candratvam |
vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇīty eva satyam || ChUp_6,4.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'The red colour of the moon is the form of <s>tejas</s>. Its white colour is that of water. Its dark colour is that of food. Thus has the moon-ness departed from the moon. The modification is merely a verbal designation, a name — only the three colours are real.' (ChUp 6.4.3) 'The red colour of lightning is the form of <s>tejas</s>. Its white colour is that of water. Its dark colour is that of food. Thus has the lightning-ness departed from lightning. The modification is merely a verbal designation, a name — only the three colours are real.' (ChUp 6.4.4)

children.text:
yad vidyuto rohitaṃ rūpaṃ tejasas tad rūpam |
yac chuklaṃ tad apām |
yat kṛṣṇaṃ tad annasya |
apāgād vidyuto vidyuttvam |
vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ trīṇi rūpāṇīty eva satyam || ChUp_6,4.4 ||

ChUpBh_6,4.2,3,4 tathā yadādityasya yaccandramaso yadvidyuta ityādi samānam /
nanu yathā nu khalu somyemāstisro devatāsrivṛttrivṛdekaikā bhavati tanme vijānīhityuktvā tejasa eva caturbhirapyudāharaṇairagnyādibhisrivṛtkaraṇaṃ darśitaṃ nābannayorudāharaṇaṃ darśitaṃ trivṛtkaraṇe /
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
abannaviṣayāṇyapyudāharaṇānyevameva ca draṣṭavyānīti manyate śrutiḥ /
tejasa udāharaṇamupalakṣaṇārtham /
rūpavattvātspaṣṭārthatvopapatteśca /
gandharasayoranudāharaṇaṃ trayāṇāmasambhavāt /
na hi gandharasau tejasi staḥ /
sparśaśabdayoranudāharaṇaṃ vibhāgena darśayitumaśakyatvāt /
yadi sarvaṃ jagattrivṛtkṛtamityagnyādivattrīṇi rūpāṇītyeva satyamagneragnitvavadapāgājjagato jagattvam /
tathānnasyāpyapśuṅgatvādāpa ityeva satyaṃ vācārambhaṇamātramannam /
tathāpāmapi tejaḥśuṅgatvādvācārambhaṇatvaṃ teja ityeva satyam /
tejaso 'pi sacchuṅgatvādvācārambhaṇatvaṃ sadityeva satyamityeṣor'tho vivakṣitaḥ /
nanu vāyvantarikṣe tvatrivṛtkṛte tejaḥ prabhṛtiṣvanantarbhūtatvādavaśiṣyete /
evaṃ gandharasaśabdasparśāścāvaśiṣṭā iti kathaṃ satā vijñātena sarvamanyadvijñātaṃ bhavettadvijñāne vā prakārāntaraṃ vācyam /
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
rūpavaddravye sarvasya darśanāt /
tejasi tāvadrūpavati śabdasparśayorapyulabhbhādvāyvantarikṣayostatra sparśaśabdaguṇavatoḥ sadbhāvo 'numīyate /
tathābannayo rūpavato rasagandhāntabhāva iti /
rūpavatāṃ trayāṇāṃ tejobannānāṃ trivṛtkaraṇapradarśanena sarvaṃ tadantarbhūtaṃ sadvikāratvāt rūpatrayavat vijñātaṃ manyate śrutiḥ /
na hi mūrtaṃ rūpavaddravyaṃ pratyākhyāya vāyvākāśayostadguṇayorgandharasayorvā grahaṇamasti /
children.translated_text: For apart from material substances having visible form, there is no apprehension of wind, space, their qualities, or of taste and smell.

children.text: athavā rūpavatāmapi trivṛtkaraṇaṃ pradarśanārthameva manyate śrutiḥ /
children.translated_text: Alternatively, the <s>śruti</s> considers the tripartite making even of substances having form to be merely illustrative.

children.text: yathā tu trivṛtkṛte trīṇi rūpāṇītyeva satyaṃ tathā pañcīkaraṇe 'pi samāno nyāya ityataḥ sarvasya sadvikāratvātsatā vijñātena sarvamidaṃ vijñātaṃ syātsadekamevādvitīyaṃ satyamiti siddhameva bhavati /
children.translated_text: Just as in the tripartite making 'only the three colours are real,' so too the same principle applies in the fivefold making (<s>pañcīkaraṇa</s>) — therefore, since everything is a modification of <s>Sat</s>, by knowing <s>Sat</s> all this would be known; '<s>Sat</s> is one alone without a second' — this is truly the reality — this is established.

children.text: tadekasminsati vijñāte sarvamidaṃ vijñātaṃ bhavatīti sūktam //2-4 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, when that one <s>Sat</s> is known, all this becomes known — this is well said. (2-4)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.4.2-4:] Similarly, 'the [red colour] of the sun,' 'of the moon,' 'of lightning' — and so on — the same [explanation applies]. Objection: Having said 'Learn from me how each of these three deities becomes tripartite,' the tripartite making has been illustrated with four examples — fire and the rest — only for <s>tejas</s> (fire/heat), but no illustration has been given for water and food in [demonstrating] the tripartite making. [Reply:] This is no fault. The <s>śruti</s> considers that illustrations regarding water and food should be understood in the same way. The illustration of <s>tejas</s> is intended to be representative. [This is] because it has visible form, and because its meaning is clearly established. Taste and smell are not illustrated because the presence of all three [colours] in them is impossible — for taste and smell do not exist in fire. Touch and sound are not illustrated because they cannot be shown in a differentiated manner. If the entire universe has been made tripartite — just as with fire and the rest, 'only the three colours are real' — just as fire-ness has departed from fire, so has world-ness departed from the world. Similarly, food too, being traceable to water, is merely a verbal designation — 'water' alone is the reality. Similarly, water too, being traceable to fire, is merely a verbal designation — 'fire' alone is the reality. And fire too, being traceable to <s>Sat</s> (Being), is merely a verbal designation — '<s>Sat</s>' alone is the reality — this is the intended meaning. Objection: But wind and space, not being made tripartite, remain outside of fire and the rest — likewise taste, smell, sound, and touch remain outside. So how could everything be known by knowing <s>Sat</s>? Or else another method must be stated for knowing them. [Reply:] This is no fault. Because in substances having visible form, everything is observed. In fire, which has visible form, sound and touch too are apprehended — therefore the existence of wind and space, which possess the qualities of touch and sound, is inferred therein. Similarly, in water and food, which have visible form, taste and smell are included. By demonstrating the tripartite making of the three [elements] that have visible form — fire, water, and food — the <s>śruti</s> considers that everything included therein is known, just like the three colours, because everything is a modification of <s>Sat</s>.

children.text: START ChUp 6,4.5
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.4.5]

children.text:
etad dha sma vai tadvidvāṃsa āhuḥ pūrve mahāśālā mahāśrotriyāḥ |
na no 'dya kaścanāśrutam amatam avijñātam udāhariṣyati |
iti hy ebhyo vidāṃ cakruḥ || ChUp_6,4.5 ||
children.translated_text: 'This indeed those ancient, great householders and great scholars who knew this used to say: "No one will now bring to us anything unheard, unthought, or unknown." For from these [three colours] they knew.' (ChUp 6.4.5)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,4.5 etadvidvāṃso viditavantaḥ pūrve 'tikrāntā mahāśālā mahāśroṇiyā āhurha sma vai kila /
kimuktavanta ityāhana no 'smākaṃ kule 'dyedānīṃ yathoktavijñānavatāṃ kaśna kaścidapyaśrutamamatamavijñātamudāhariṣyati nodāhariṣyati sarvaṃ vijñātamevāsmatkulīnānāṃ sadvijñānavattvādityābhiprāyaḥ /
te punaḥ kathaṃ sarvaṃ vijñātavanta ityāha-ebhyasribhyo rohitādirūpebhyasrivṛtkṛtebhyo vijñātebhyaḥ sarvamapyanyacchiṣṭamevameveti vidāñcakrurvijñātavanto yasmāttasmātsarvajñā eva sadvijñānātta āsurityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.4.5:] Those who knew this — who had understood it — those ancient ones of the past, great householders and great scholars, used to say indeed. What did they say? — the text states: 'No one will now — at present — bring to us, in our family, who possess knowledge as described — no one at all — anything unheard, unthought, or unknown.' 'Everything is known indeed by the members of our family, because of their knowledge of <s>Sat</s>' — this is the purport. How then did they know everything? The text says: from these three — the red and other colours — which have been made tripartite, being known, everything else too was known in the same way — they knew, they understood — because of that they were indeed omniscient through the knowledge of <s>Sat</s> — this is the meaning.

children.text: athavaibhyo vidāñcakrurityagnyādibhyo dṛṣṭāntebhyo vijñātebhyaḥ sarvamanyadvidāñcakrurityetat //5 //
children.translated_text: Alternatively, 'from these they knew' means: from these illustrations of fire and the rest, having known them, they knew everything else. (5)

children.text: START ChUp 6,4.6
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.4.6]

children.text:
yad u rohitam ivābhūd iti tejasas tad rūpam iti tad vidāṃ cakruḥ |
yad u śuklam ivābhūd ity apāṃ rūpam iti tad vidāṃ cakruḥ |
yad u kṛṣṇam ivābhūd ity annasya rūpam iti tad vidāṃ cakruḥ || ChUp_6,4.6 ||
children.translated_text: 'Whatever appeared reddish — they knew it was the form of <s>tejas</s>. Whatever appeared whitish — they knew it was the form of water. Whatever appeared darkish — they knew it was the form of food.' (ChUp 6.4.6)

children.text:
yad v avijñātam ivābhūd ity etāsām eva devatānāṃ samāsa iti tad vidāṃ cakruḥ |
yathā nu khalu somyemās tisro devatāḥ puruṣaṃ prāpya trivṛt trivṛd ekaikā bhavati tan me vijānīhīti || ChUp_6,4.7 ||
children.translated_text: 'Whatever appeared as if unknown — they knew it was a combination of these very deities. Now learn from me, dear one, how each of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes tripartite.' (ChUp 6.4.7)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,4.6,7 katham /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.4.6-7:] How?

children.text: yadanyadrūpeṇa sandihyamāne kapotādirūpe rohitamiva yadgṛhyamāṇamabhūtteṣāṃ pūrveṣāṃ brahmavidāṃ tattejaso rūpamiti vidāñcakruḥ tathā yacchuklamivābhūdgṛhyamāṇaṃ tadāpāṃ rūpaṃ yatkṛṣṇamiva gṛhyamāṇaṃ tadannasyeti vidāñcakrurevamevātyantadurlakṣyaṃ yadu apyavijñātamiva viśeṣato 'gṛhyamāṇamabhūttadapyetāsāmeva tisṛṇāṃ devatānāṃ samāsaḥ samudāya iti vidāñcakruḥ /
children.translated_text: When there was doubt about the colour of something like a pigeon — whatever was apprehended as appearing reddish — those ancient knowers of <s>Brahman</s> knew it was the form of <s>tejas</s>. Similarly, whatever appeared whitish, they knew it was the form of water. Whatever appeared darkish, they knew it was the form of food. In the same way, even that which was extremely difficult to discern — whatever appeared as if unknown, not specifically apprehended — even that they knew to be a combination, an aggregate, of these very three deities.

children.text: evaṃ tāvadbāhyaṃ vastvagnyādivavijñātaṃ tathedānīṃ yathā nu khalu he somyemā yathoktāstisro devatāḥ puraṣaṃ śiraḥpāmyādilakṣaṇaṃ kāryakāraṇasaṅghātaṃ prāpya puruṣeṇopayujyamānāsrivṛttrivṛdekaikā bhavati tanme vijānīhi nigadata ityuktvā'ha //6-7 //
children.translated_text: Thus, external objects like fire and the rest have been understood [as tripartite]. Now [the text says]: 'Now, dear one, learn from me how indeed these three deities as described, upon reaching a person — the aggregate of body and organs characterized by head, feet, and so forth — being utilized by the person, each becomes tripartite.' Having said this, [the father] spoke. (6-7)

children.text: iti cchāndogyopaniṣadi ṣaṣṭhādhyāyasya caturthaḥ khaṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth section of the sixth chapter of the <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>.

children.text: START ChUp 6,5.1
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.5.1]

children.text:
annam aśitaṃ tredhā vidhīyate |
tasya yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātus tat purīṣaṃ bhavati |
yo madhyamas tan māṃsam |
yo 'ṇiṣṭhas tan manaḥ || ChUp_6,5.1 ||
children.translated_text: 'Food, when eaten, is divided threefold. Its coarsest constituent becomes excrement. The middle one becomes flesh. The subtlest becomes mind.' (ChUp 6.5.1)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,5.1 annamaśitaṃ bhuktaṃ tredhā vidhīyate jāṭharemāgninā pacyamānaṃ tridhā vibhajyate /
kathaṃ, tasyānnasya tridhā vidhīyamānasya yaḥ sthaviṣṭhaḥ sthūlatamo dhātuḥ sthūlatamaṃ vastu vibhaktasya sthūloṃ'śastatpurīṣaṃ bhavati /
yo madhyamoṃ'śo dhāturannasya tadrasādikrameṇa pariṇamya māṃsaṃ bhavati yo 'ṇiṣṭho 'ṇutamo dhātuḥ sa ūrdhvaṃ hṛdayaṃ prāpya sūkṣmāsu hitākhyāsu nāḍīpvanupravisya vāgādikaraṇasaṅghātasya sthitimutpādayanmano bhavati manorūpeṇa vipariṇamanmanasa upacayaṃ karoti /
tataścānnopacitatvānmanaso bhautikatvameva na vaiśeṣikatantroktalakṣaṇaṃ nityaṃ niravayaṃ ceti gṛhyate /
children.translated_text: From this, since the mind is nourished by food, its material nature (<s>bhautikatva</s>) alone is established — not that it is eternal and partless as described in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system.

children.text: yadapi mano 'sya daivaṃ cakṣuriti vakṣyati tadapi na nityatvāpekṣayā kiṃ tarhi sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭādisarvendriyaviṣayavyāpakatvāpekṣayā /
children.translated_text: And when [the text] will say 'The mind is its divine eye,' that too is not with reference to the mind's eternality, but rather with reference to its capacity to pervade all objects of the senses — subtle, concealed, distant, and so on.

children.text: yaccānyendriyaviṣayāpekṣayā nityatvaṃ tadapyāpekṣikameveti vakṣyāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: And whatever eternality [is attributed to the mind] in comparison with the objects of other senses — that too is only relative, as we shall explain.

children.text: sadekamevādvitīyamiti śruteḥ //1 //
children.translated_text: Because of the <s>śruti</s>: 'Being (<s>Sat</s>) is one alone, without a second.' (1)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.5.1:] Food that is eaten, when being digested by the gastric fire (<s>jāṭharāgni</s>), is divided threefold. How? Of that food being divided threefold, the coarsest constituent — the grossest substance, the gross portion of what has been separated — becomes excrement (<s>purīṣa</s>). The middle portion, the constituent of food, transforming through the stages of juice (<s>rasa</s>) and the rest, becomes flesh. The subtlest, the most minute constituent, rising upward, reaching the heart, entering the subtle channels called <s>hitā nāḍīs</s>, producing the stability of the aggregate of organs such as speech — becomes mind; transforming into the form of mind, it nourishes the mind.

children.text: START ChUp 6,5.2
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.5.2]

children.text:
āpaḥ pītās tredhā vidhīyante |
tāsāṃ yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātus tan mūtraṃ bhavati |
yo madhyamas tal lohitam |
yo 'ṇiṣṭhaḥ sa prāṇaḥ || ChUp_6,5.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'Water that is drunk is divided threefold. Of it, the coarsest constituent becomes urine. The middle one becomes blood. The subtlest becomes <s>prāṇa</s> (life-breath).' (ChUp 6.5.2)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,5.2 tathā'paḥ pītāstredhā vidhīyante tāsāṃ yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātustanmūtraṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.5.2:] Similarly, water that is drunk is divided threefold. Of it, the coarsest constituent becomes urine.

children.text: yo madhyamastallohitaṃ bhavati /
children.translated_text: The middle one becomes blood.

children.text: yo 'ṇiṣṭhaḥ sa prāṇo bhavati /
children.translated_text: The subtlest becomes <s>prāṇa</s>.

children.text: vakṣyati hyāpomayaḥ prāṇo na pibato vicchetsyata iti //2//
children.translated_text: For [the text] will say: '<s>Prāṇa</s> is made of water; if one does not drink, it will be cut off.' (2)

children.text: START ChUp 6,5.3
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.5.3]

children.text:
tejo 'śitaṃ tredhā vidhīyate |
tasya yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātus tad asthi bhavati |
yo madhyamaḥ sa majjā |
yo 'ṇiṣṭhaḥ sā vāk || ChUp_6,5.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'Fire (<s>tejas</s>) that is eaten is divided threefold. Of it, the coarsest constituent becomes bone. The middle one is marrow. The subtlest is speech (<s>vāk</s>).' (ChUp 6.5.3)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,5.3 tathā tejo 'śitaṃ tailaghṛtādi bhakṣitaṃ tredhā vidhīyate tasya yaḥ sthaviṣṭho dhātustadasthi bhavati /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.5.3:] Similarly, fire (<s>tejas</s>) that is eaten — oil, ghee, and the like that are consumed — is divided threefold. Of it, the coarsest constituent becomes bone.

children.text: yo madhyamaḥsa majjāsthyantargataḥ snehaḥ /
children.translated_text: The middle one is marrow — the oily substance within the bones.

children.text: yo 'ṇiṣṭhaḥ sā vāk /
children.translated_text: The subtlest is speech.

children.text: tailaghṛtādibhakṣaṇāddhi vāgviśadā bhāṣaṇe samarthā bhavatīti prasiddhaṃ loke //3 //
children.translated_text: For it is well known in the world that by consuming oil, ghee, and the like, speech becomes clear and capable of articulation. (3)

children.text: START ChUp 6,5.4
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.5.4]

children.text:
annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ |
āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ |
tejomayī vāg iti |
bhūya eva mā bhagavān vijñāpayatv iti |
tathā somyeti hovāca || ChUp_6,5.4 ||
children.translated_text: 'Thus, dear one, the mind is made of food. <s>Prāṇa</s> is made of water. Speech is made of fire.' 'Please explain further to me, Blessed One.' 'So be it, dear one,' he said. (ChUp 6.5.4)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,5.4 yata evamannamayaṃ hi somya mana āpomayaḥ prāṇastejomayī vāk /
nanu kevalānnabhakṣiṇa ākhuprabhṛtayo vāgminaḥ prāṇavantaśca tathāṃmātrabhakṣyāḥ sāmudrā mīnamakaraprabhṛtayo manasvino vāggminaśca tathā snehapānāmapi prāṇavattvaṃ cānumeyaṃ yadi santi tatra kathamannamayaṃ hi somya mana ityādyucyate /
naiṣa doṣaḥ /
sarvasya trivṛtkṛtatvātsarvatra sarvopapatteḥ /
na hyatrivṛtkṛtamannamaśnāti kaścidāpo vātrivṛtkṛtāḥ pīyante tejo vātrivṛtkṛtamaśnāti kaścidityannādānāmākhuprabhṛtīnāṃ vāggmitvaṃ prāṇavattvaṃ cetyādyaviruddham /
children.translated_text: For no one eats food that has not been made threefold, nor drinks water that has not been made threefold, nor eats fire that has not been made threefold — therefore, it is not contradictory that food-eaters like mice possess speech and <s>prāṇa</s>.

children.text: ityevaṃ pratyāyitaḥ śveketurāha-bhūya eva punareva mā māṃ bhagavānannamayaṃ hi somya mana ityādi vijñāpayatu dṛṣṭāntenāvagamayu nādyāpi mamāsminnarthe samyaṅniścayo jātaḥ /
children.translated_text: Thus convinced, <s>Śvetaketu</s> says: 'Please explain further to me, Blessed One' — [meaning:] 'Demonstrate [this teaching] \"the mind is made of food, dear one\" and so forth with an illustration, for even now I have not yet reached complete certainty in this matter.'

children.text: yasmāttejovannamayatvenāviśiṣṭe deha ekasminnupayujyamānānyannāpsnehajātānyaṇiṣṭhadhāturūpeṇa manaḥprāṇavāca upacinvanti svajātyanatikrameṇeti durvijñeyamityabhiprāyo 'to bhūya evetyādyāha /
children.translated_text: Since in a single body that is undifferentiated as to fire, food, and water, the food, water, and oily substances that are consumed nourish the mind, <s>prāṇa</s>, and speech respectively in the form of the subtlest constituent, without transgressing their own kind — this is difficult to understand — such is the purport. Therefore he says 'please explain further' and so on.

children.text: tamevamuktavantaṃ tathāstu somyeti hovāca pitā śṛṇvatra dṛṣṭāntaṃ yathaitadupapadyate yatpṛcchasi //4//
children.translated_text: To him who spoke thus, the father said: 'So be it, dear one' — listen to the illustration by which what you ask is established. (4)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.5.4:] Since this is so — the mind is indeed made of food, dear one; <s>prāṇa</s> is made of water; speech is made of fire. Now, [one might object:] creatures that eat food alone, such as mice and the like, are [also] endowed with speech and <s>prāṇa</s>; likewise, aquatic creatures that eat only water, such as fish, crocodiles, and the like, are endowed with mind and speech; and similarly, from those who drink only oily substances, the possession of <s>prāṇa</s> can also be inferred — if such beings exist, how can it be said 'the mind is made of food, dear one' and so on? This is not a fault — because everything has been made threefold (<s>trivṛtkṛta</s>), [the presence of] everything everywhere is established.

children.text: iti cchāndogyopaniṣadi ṣaṣṭhādhyāyasya pañcamaḥ khaṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fifth section of the sixth chapter of the <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>.

children.text: START ChUp 6,6.1
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.6.1]

children.text:
dadhnaḥ somya mathyamānasya yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati |
tat sarpir bhavati || ChUp_6,6.1 ||
children.translated_text: 'Of curds being churned, dear one, the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes butter.' (ChUp 6.6.1)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,6.1 dadhnaḥ somya mathyamānasya yo 'ṇimāṇubhāvaḥ sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati sambhūyordhvaṃ navanūtabhāvena gacchati tatsarpirbhavati //1 //
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.6.1:] Of curds being churned, dear one, the subtle essence — the minute part — rises upward, gathering together and rising upward in the form of fresh butter. That becomes clarified butter (<s>sarpis</s>). (1)

children.text: START ChUp 6,6.2
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.6.2]

children.text:
evam eva khalu somyānnasyāśyamānasya yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati |
tan mano bhavati || ChUp_6,6.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'In the same way, dear one, of food being eaten, the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes mind.' (ChUp 6.6.2)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,6.2 yathāyaṃ dṛṣṭānta evameva khalu somyānnasyaudanāderaśyamānasya bhujyamānasyodaryemāgninā vāyusahiteta khajeneva mathyamānasya yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati tanmano bhavati mano 'vayavaiḥ saha sambhūya mana upacinotītyetat //2 //
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.6.2:] Just as this illustration — in the same way indeed, dear one, of food such as cooked rice being eaten, being consumed — being churned, as it were, by the gastric fire aided by wind, like [curds] by a churning rod — the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes mind — gathering together with the parts of mind, it nourishes the mind. This is the meaning. (2)

children.text: START ChUp 6,6.3
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.6.3]

children.text:
apāṃ somya pīyamānānāṃ yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati |
sā prāno bhavati || ChUp_6,6.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'Of water being drunk, dear one, the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes <s>prāṇa</s>.' (ChUp 6.6.3)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,6.3 tathāpāṃ somya pīyamānānāṃ yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati sa prāṇo bhavatīti //3 //
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.6.3:] Similarly, of water being drunk, dear one, the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes <s>prāṇa</s>. (3)

children.text: START ChUp 6,6.4
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.6.4]

children.text:
tejasaḥ somyāśyamānasya yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati |
sā vāg bhavati || ChUp_6,6.4 ||
children.translated_text: 'Of fire being eaten, dear one, the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes speech.' (ChUp 6.6.4)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,6.4 evameva khalu somya tejaso 'śyamānasya yo 'ṇimā sa ūrdhvaḥ samudīṣati sā vāgbhavati //4 //
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.6.4:] In the same way indeed, dear one, of fire being eaten, the subtle essence rises upward. That becomes speech. (4)

children.text: START ChUp 6,6.5
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.6.5]

children.text:
annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ |
āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ |
tejomayī vāg iti |
bhūya eva mā bhagavān vijñāpayatv iti |
tathā somyeti hovāca || ChUp_6,6.5 ||
children.translated_text: 'Thus, dear one, the mind is made of food. <s>Prāṇa</s> is made of water. Speech is made of fire.' 'Please explain further to me, Blessed One.' 'So be it, dear one,' he said. (ChUp 6.6.5)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,6.5 annamayaṃ hi somya mana āpomayaḥ prāṇastejomayī vāgiti yuktameva mayoktamityamiprāyaḥ /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.6.5:] 'The mind is made of food, dear one; <s>prāṇa</s> is made of water; speech is made of fire' — the purport is: what I have said is indeed well-established.

children.text: ato 'ptejasorastvetatsarvamevam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, regarding water and fire, all this is just so.

children.text: manastvannamayamityatra naikāntena mama niścayo jāto 'to bhūya eva mā bhagavānmanaso 'nnamayatvaṃ dṛṣṭāntena vijñāpayatviti /
children.translated_text: But regarding the mind being made of food — in this I have not yet reached complete certainty. Therefore, please explain further to me, Blessed One, the food-made nature of the mind with an illustration.

children.text: tathā somyeti hovāca pitā //5//
children.translated_text: 'So be it, dear one,' the father said. (5)

children.text: iti cchāndogyopaniṣadi ṣaṣṭhādhyāyasya ṣaṣṭhaḥ khaṇḍaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the sixth section of the sixth chapter of the <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s>.

children.text: START ChUp 6,7.1
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.7.1]

children.text:
ṣoḍaśakalaḥ somya puruṣaḥ |
pañcadaśāhāni māśīḥ |
kāmam apaḥ piba |
āpomayaḥ prāṇo na pibato vicchetsyata iti || ChUp_6,7.1 ||
children.translated_text: 'A person, dear one, consists of sixteen parts. Do not eat for fifteen days. Drink water as you wish. <s>Prāṇa</s>, being made of water, will not be cut off if you drink.' (ChUp 6.7.1)

children.text:
ChUpBh_6,7.1 annasya bhuktasya yo 'ṇiṣṭho dhātuḥ sa manasi śaktimadhāt sānnopacitā manasaḥ śaktiḥ ṣoḍaśadhā pravibhajya puruṣasya kalātvena nirdidikṣitā /
tayā manasyannopacitayā śaktyā ṣoḍaśadhā pravibhaktayā saṃyuktastadvānkāryakaraṇasaṅghātalakṣaṇo jīvaviśiṣṭaḥ piṇḍaḥ puruṣaḥ ṣoḍaśakala ucyate yasyāṃ satyāṃ draṣṭā śrotā mantā boddhā kartā vijñātā sarvakriyāsamarthaḥ puruṣo bhavati hīyamānāyāṃ ca yasyāṃ sāmarthyahāniḥ /
vakṣyati"cāthānnasyā'yī draṣṭe"tyādi /
sarvasya kāryakaraṇasya sāmarthyaṃ manaḥkṛtameva /
mānasena hi balena sampannā balino dṛśyante loke, dhyānāhārāśca kecidannasya sarvātmakatvāt /
children.translated_text: For in the world, those endowed with mental strength are seen to be strong; and some [subsist] on meditation-food — because food is the self of all.

children.text: ato 'nnakṛtaṃ mānasaṃ vīryaṃ ṣoḍaśa kalā yasya puruṣasya so 'yaṃ ṣoḍaśakalaḥ puruṣaḥ etaccetpratyakṣīkartumicchasi pañcadaśasaṃkhyākānyahāni māśīraśanaṃ mā kārṣīḥ /
children.translated_text: Therefore, this person of sixteen parts — whose sixteen parts constitute the mental vigor produced by food — if you wish to perceive this directly, do not eat for fifteen days.

children.text: kāmamicchāto 'paḥ piba yasmānnapibato 'paste prāṇo vicchetsyate vicchedamāpatsyate yasmādāpomayo 'bvikāraḥ prāṇa ityavocāma /
children.translated_text: Drink water as you wish, because if you do not drink, <s>prāṇa</s> will be cut off — will come to cessation — since we have said that <s>prāṇa</s> is made of water, a modification of water.

children.text: na hi kāryaṃ svakāraṇopaṣṭambhamantareṇāvibhraṃśamānaṃ sthātumutsahate //1 //
children.translated_text: For an effect cannot remain without disintegrating in the absence of the support of its own cause. (1)

[<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.7.1:] The subtlest constituent of food that is eaten contributes power to the mind. That power, nourished by food, is intended to be demonstrated as the sixteen parts of a person, divided sixteenfold. Endowed with that power nourished by food in the mind, divided sixteenfold — the embodied aggregate characterized by the body-organ complex, distinguished by the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) — is called a person of sixteen parts. When that [power] exists, the person becomes a seer, hearer, thinker, knower, doer, understander — capable of all activities. And when it diminishes, there is a loss of capacity. [The text] will say: 'Then he does not see' and so on. The capacity of the entire body-organ complex is indeed produced by the mind.

children.text: START ChUp 6,7.2
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.7.2]

children.text:
sa ha pañcadaśāhāni nāśa |
atha hainam upasasāda kiṃ bravīmi bho iti |
ṛcaḥ somya yajūṃṣi sāmānīti |
sa hovāca na vai mā pratibhānti bho iti || ChUp_6,7.2 ||
children.translated_text: 'He did not eat for fifteen days. Then he approached [his father] and said: "What shall I recite, sir?" "The <s>Ṛc</s> verses, the <s>Yajus</s> formulas, the <s>Sāman</s> chants, dear one." He replied: "They do not come to my mind, sir."' (ChUp 6.7.2)

children.text: ChUpBh_6,7.2 sa haivaṃ śrutvā manaso 'nnamayatvaṃ pratyakṣīkartuṃmicchanpañcadaśāhāni nā'śāśanaṃ na kṛtavān /
children.translated_text: [<s>Śaṅkara's</s> commentary on 6.7.2:] He, having heard this and wishing to perceive directly the food-made nature of the mind, did not eat for fifteen days — he did not take food.

children.text: atha ṣoḍaśe 'hani hainaṃ pitaramupasasādopagatavānupagamya covāca kiṃ bravīmi bho iti /
children.translated_text: Then, on the sixteenth day, he approached his father and having approached, said: 'What shall I recite, sir?'

children.text: itara āha ṛcaḥ somya yajūṃṣi sāmānyadhīṣveti /
children.translated_text: The other [the father] said: 'Recite the <s>Ṛc</s> verses, the <s>Yajus</s> formulas, the <s>Sāman</s> chants, dear one.'

children.text: evamuktaḥ pitrā'ha-na vai mā māmṛgādīni mama manasi na dṛśyanta ityartho he bho bhagavanniti //2//
children.translated_text: Thus told by his father, he said: 'They do not [come to mind]' — meaning: 'The <s>Ṛg</s> verses and the rest do not appear in my mind' — 'sir, Blessed One.' (2)

children.text: START ChUp 6,7.3
children.translated_text: [Beginning of <s>Chāndogya Upaniṣad</s> 6.7.3]

children.text:
taṃ hovāca yathā somya mahato 'bhyāhitasyaiko 'ṅgāraḥ khadyotamātraḥ pariśiṣṭaḥ syāt |
tena tato 'pi na bahu dahet |
evaṃ somya te ṣoḍaśānāṃ kalānām ekā kalā atiśiṣṭā syāt |
tayaitarhi vedān nānubhavasi |
aśāna |
atha me vijñāsyasīti || ChUp_6,7.3 ||
children.translated_text: 'He said to him: "Just as, dear one, of a great fire that has been built up, if a single ember the size of a firefly were left over, by that it would not burn much more than that — so, dear one, of your sixteen parts, one part may be left over. By that you do not now apprehend the <s>Vedas</s>. Eat, then you will understand me."' (ChUp 6.7.3)
